title: MicroRemedy Conductor: Incremental runbook-to-task compiler with safety gates
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Problem: Oncall engineers spend significant time executing multi-step runbooks manually; existing runbook fragments are brittle and often not idempotent. Objective: build a lightweight compiler (MicroRemedy Conductor) that converts canonical runbook steps into atomic, idempotent tasks with runtime safety gates, a dry-run simulator, and per-step telemetry. This ticket delivers the initial compiler + runtime hooks for safe, incremental rollout to firstline oncall and support tooling.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Compiler converts a subset of canonical runbook DSL (checks, remediation calls, rollbacks) into atomic task artifacts; 2) Each generated task is idempotent or annotated with a compensating action; 3) Runtime exposes a dry-run mode that simulates state changes and emits a semantic diff; 4) Per-step telemetry (latency, token/cost, success rate) surfaces in Grafana dashboard; 5) Safety gates allow feature-flagged canary release and manual abort by oncall; 6) Automated unit + integration tests with >=90% coverage for the compiler core.
implementation_notes:
Technical approach:
- Parser: reuse existing runbook snippets registry to extract linearized step graph.
- Compiler: translate steps into TaskSpec JSON (op, inputs, outputs, idempotency hints, compensator). TaskSpec is intentionally minimal to avoid runtime coupling.
- Runtime shim: run tasks in an isolated container for mutable steps and use stateful dry-run for non-destructive validation.
- Safety gating: integrate with flags service (ff.redwood) to control canary pop sets; support runtime explicit aborts and timeouts.
- Telemetry: emit step-level traces and metrics (step.latency_ms, step.success, step.retries, step.cost_tokens). Tag traces with run_id, task_id, team.
- Testing: add simulator harness (simulates cloud resources and returns semantic diffs).
- Backwards compatibility: generated TaskSpec should include original runbook reference and line mappings for traceability.
progress_updates: 2026-03-02: Spike completed. Parser prototype can ingest 3 common runbook step patterns (check, remediate, verify).
2026-03-05: Decided to emit TaskSpec as flat JSON to keep runtime language-agnostic; removed attempt to embed KV-cache semantics in initial release.
2026-03-09: Implemented dry-run simulator with semantic diff output; early integration tests against sandbox show no destructive operations in dry-run mode.
2026-03-12: Safety gating integrated with ff.redwood; enabling canary for 5% of oncall team. Preparing PR for review.
comments: PM Review (Rosa Chen): Add explicit UX callback for oncall to 'request human approval' before destructive tasks; prioritize by customer-impact in rollout.

Design Feedback (Mina Patel): Suggested adding a compact runbook timeline view in Console that highlights compiler-generated atomic tasks and their compensators. Filed DES-1242 (placeholder) for Console mockups.

Engineering Review (K. Stone): Concern about stateful dry-run complexity. Proposal: limit dry-run to a mocked resource layer for v1 and document assumptions clearly in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/MicroRemedy+Design.
Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-runbook-compiler/pull/128 (WIP; includes parser + TaskSpec emitter).
Benchmark Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/G7xyz/microremedy-step-telemetry (showing simulator latencies and early success-rates).
QA Note (Leah Ortiz): Need an automated chaos test that flips FF gating during execution to validate abort semantics. QA will author tests in cycle 2026-W11.

Security (R. Ng): Marked for security review because compiler emits runbook references and may include sensitive resource identifiers in logs. Set security_review_required=true and added masking in telemetry pipeline.
risks_and_mitigation: Risks: accidental destructive ops during initial rollout; noisy telemetry with PII; complexity of idempotency for external APIs. Mitigations: start with read-only and safe remediation steps, require human approval for high-risk tasks, scrub identifiers before emitting metrics, and provide compensating actions for every generated task.
